body_html:
How to think about it

An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in energy levels (shells and subshells: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ …). Isotopes have the same number of protons but different neutrons; relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of the isotopes, measured with a mass spectrometer.

When excited electrons fall to lower levels they emit photons of fixed energies: this gives line spectra and flame colours. Atomic absorption spectroscopy, invented at CSIRO, measures metal concentrations.

Across a period nuclear charge rises, so atoms shrink and hold electrons more tightly; down a group atoms get bigger and lose outer electrons more easily.

Example

Copper: ⁶³Cu 69.2%, ⁶⁵Cu 30.8%. Ar?

(63 × 69.2 + 65 × 30.8) ÷ 100

Answer: 63.6

Example

Electron configuration of S (Z = 16)?

2 + 8 + 6

1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴

Answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴

Common mistakes

  • Using the mass number of the most common isotope as Ar.
  • Thinking atoms get bigger across a period: they get smaller.
  • Saying the electrons ‘burn’ in a flame test: they are excited and then emit light.

faq.q: Why does each element have its own emission spectrum?
faq.a: Each element has its own set of electron energy levels, so the energy differences, and the colours of light emitted, are unique to it.

faq.q: Why does ionisation energy decrease down a group?
faq.a: The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, so less energy is needed to remove it.

items.q: Arsenic (As) and calcium (Ca) are in the same period. Which has the larger atomic radius?

items.q: Which has the larger atomic radius, Li or K?

items.q: On what is the modern periodic law based?

items.q: Which is the largest ion: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ or F⁻?
